segments.en: The chapter culminates (entry 65) in the vision of Mashiach: the Second Temple was destroyed through baseless hatred — and the rebuilt Temple will stand on the foundation of love and totality. Eliyahu's mission is to make peace — and through peace the halachah will be clarified and the redemption will come.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

The chapter's central paradox is stated with great boldness: the highest form of joy is not the joy of good fortune — it is the conversion of grief and sighing themselves into joy. The Sitra Achara and husks are called "halls of exchange" — they exchange everything. The antidote is to exchange back: to take the grief they introduce and convert it to the source of joy. This is the aspect of the chelbonah in the incense — unpleasant smelling yet part of the holy compound.

The practical teaching is striking: specifically at the moment when sadness intensifies — when one is most aware of one's distance and failures — one should rejoice most. The very awareness that a person as distant as oneself still merits to put on tefilin — that is itself a cause for profound joy. This is described as the essential perfection of the mitzvah — not performing it from a place of calm virtue, but wresting joy from the depths of one's awareness of unworthiness.

Entry 7 explains why words of foolishness can produce genuine joy: the joy is in exile, clothed in wordly speech. When a Jewish person reaches joy through apparently foolish words — they are actually elevating sparks of the Shechinah's joy from its exile. The joy is real — only its clothing is foolish.

The chapter culminates in a vision of redemption driven by joy: as Israel multiply and each elevates their portion of joy from the depths of the husks — until the feet are raised from the hold of death — Mashiach arrives and the grief and sighing flee forever.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

A compact ten-entry chapter, largely a series of cross-references anchored by three substantive entries. The essential teaching is the kabbalistic distinction between two modes of wine: the yayin hamashkei'r — intoxicating wine — which withdraws the seventy faces of Torah from the mind and makes all paths seem smooth (the delusion that one is always right), and the yayin hamesame'ach — the wine that truly gladdens — which is the aspect of holy da'as and awakened spiritual awareness. Whether any given act of drinking yields the one or the other depends on the person's rectification of the bris.

Entry 10 gives the sharpest warning: a drunk person is forbidden to rule on halachah — because their deviation from truth is invisible to themselves. The danger is not just foolish speech — it is the subtle distortion whereby truth appears fully possessed while actually slipping away.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

This rich chapter reveals that sleep is not merely rest — it is a profound spiritual event. On one side: shainah echad mishishim b'misah — sleep is one sixtieth of death — the mochin withdraw, the Sitra Achara rests on the hands, and false beliefs can penetrate. On the other side: sleep is the aspect of bitul el ha'tachlis — nullification toward the purpose — and during this nullification the soul ascends to the World to Come, renews itself in the womb of supernal faith, and returns with new mochin.

The Krias Shema before sleep — and the declaration of mesirat nefesh within it — is what enables the soul to enter the holy gates of faith during sleep rather than fall to the externals. The morning handwashing is then the reclamation of the renewed da'as from the World to Come — actively driving away the contamination that attached during sleep.

Entry 34 is the most mystically profound: the sleep of the true Tzadik is a cosmic act — their soul's ascent during sleep triggers a supernal union that clarifies the holy sparks from among the nations — and through this, distant and wicked souls are moved to teshuvah without even knowing why. The Tzadik's sleep is more spiritually productive than most people's waking hours.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

This chapter reveals the kabbalistic dimension behind one of the Torah's most practical mitzvos. Every creature contains a soul — a reincarnated human soul that fell there through sin — principally through arrogance and the flaw of the bris. The purpose of shechitah is to release and elevate that soul from the animal level — the absence of da'as — back to the human level — the presence of da'as.

The knife [chalef] carries profound symbolism: it must be perfectly smooth with no notch — the aspect of the fullness of the moon, the fullness of faith, the fullness of holy malchus. The back-and-forth motion of the slaughter corresponds to the Tzadik's movement of ratzo v'shov — also to teshuvah's requirement to pass back through one's own history before ascending.

The requirement to show the knife to the Sage is not merely legal — it is spiritually essential. Only the true Sage — who embodies living Torah — can validate that the knife carries the holiness needed to perform the rectification. And entry 13 offers a beautiful insight: fish require no shechitah because they are the aspect of the ever-watchful eye — the root of the supernal will — and the evil eye of materialistic wisdom has no dominion over them.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

The longest chapter in the volume at 115 entries — yet not exhausting, because its entries span an extraordinary range: from the most practical (establish fixed daily Torah study sessions even under heavy obstacles — entry 22) to the most cosmic (through writing a Torah scroll one elevates the entire aspect of place to above place — entry 69).

Several themes run through all 115 entries. First: the Torah is not static — it is renewed each day, each morning, through the trace-impression of sleep and nullification. The obligation of Torah study is not just to learn what was — it is to receive the Torah freshly, as though given now. Second: the essential measure of Torah is action — lav midrash iqar ela ma'aseh — "the essential is not the learning but the action." This phrase appears no fewer than eight times in the chapter. Third: scholarship and righteousness must be unified — the one who separates them causes the original flaw of the Tree of Knowledge.

Entry 49 is perhaps the most ambitious — a sweeping meditation on the clarification of truth as the essential purpose of all Torah study, all generations, all begetting of children. Truth has beginning, middle, and end — and all three are needed. This is why the Torah is threefold; why Yaakov represents the ultimate truth; why the Temple of Yaakov endures forever.

Entry 102 is the great consolation: from the day Israel received the Torah — they can never truly be separated from Hashem. The Torah descends into the deepest impurity, the lowest depths — and calls out from there: "How long, O simple ones?" Torah words do not receive impurity. There is no distance from which the Torah cannot reach.

"I said to Hashem: You are my G-d — my good is not upon You. As for the holy ones who are in the earth — and the mighty — all my desire is in them. Boundary lines have fallen for me in pleasant places — indeed my portion is beautiful to me."
Completed and finished — praise to the G-d Creator of the world.
Otzar HaYirah — Volume IV (נ–ת) | 25 Chapters | Translation completed with reverence and joy

Entries 1–6: The root of poverty and its remedy. The essential root of poverty is the lack of faith in Hashem's direct Providence — attributing everything to the way of nature. The adversary burdens people with livelihood worries so they have no time to cry to Hashem. The remedies: reciting Tehilla l'David (Psalm 145) daily with kavana; prayer breaks all evil traits especially the desire for money; and revealing the G-dliness hidden within every worldly thing draws blessing upon all one's handiwork.

Entries 7–11: Commerce as holy work — the Mishkan and bitachon. All commerce must be conducted with complete faith (emuna), for this draws the free kindness (chesed chinam) that sustained the world before Matan Torah. Business conducted with holy intent is the work of the Mishkan; its profit should be directed toward tzedaka to true tzaddikim and worthy poor. Bitachon is the aspect of gazing at Hashem — creating the vessel for flow through direct and returning light (or yashar v'or chozer). Israel's livelihood flows through holiness; the nations receive through the kelipos.

Entries 12–16: True wealth, the tzaddik, and the danger of money-desire. True wealth is receiving with ratzon from the Yam HaChachma. The desire for money is the aspect of seven years of famine — the tzaddik (the aspect of Yosef) alone repairs it through tzedaka. Blemishing the tzaddik's honor leads to money-desire and the aspect of Pharaoh. Guard against damaging another's money. Seek the true tzaddik — most of humanity searches for money when in truth they seek the tzaddik, not knowing what they search for.

Entries 17–21: The 39 melachos, Shabbos, and effortless livelihood. A person does nothing — livelihood flows through the nullification of the 39 labors and the illumination of Shabbos's ratzon that blesses all six days. When one sanctifies oneself and magnifies Hashem's Name, the 39 labors become the 39 lights (Tal Oros) — the work of the Mishkan done on its own. Torah and prayer are the source of all blessing; more Torah means less livelihood toil.

Entries 22–27: Justice, Providence, the sealed saying, and prayer. Never question Hashem's judgments in livelihood matters — this is the essential perversion of justice from which all corruptions come. All wealth flows from the Yam HaChachma; coveting blemishes the illumination of ratzon. Two types of monetary damage: theft/loss from da'as-blemish; compulsion from yira-blemish. Staying awake all night breaks money-desire. Most holy sparks are sunk in money — the tzaddik who breaks this desire extracts them all. Livelihood flows through prayer — when da'as is blemished prayer becomes judgment-prayer, and sustenance becomes as hard as splitting the Reed Sea.

Entries 28–32: The compelling force, false compassion, and holy counsel. The money burden strengthens the compelling force (koach hamachri'ach); remedy: tzedaka to worthy poor. The Sitra Achra uses false "compassion" about livelihood to burden people with heavy labor — the truly compassionate advice is to reduce business and increase Torah. All livelihood toil flows from the blemish of faith in the sages (emuna t'chachomim) through Adam's sin. The repair: draw close to the tzaddik who draws perfect counsel. Each person's trade is suited to the specific tikkun of their soul. Anger destroys wealth — cross-reference to Ka'as section.

Entries 33–40: Holy money, the poverty mindset, imagination, and tzedaka. Tzaddikim elevate all money to holiness — everything is consecrated. The essential repair of holy wealth is the poverty mindset (anivus): always holding oneself as a pauper, rejoicing in one's portion — this is true wealth and true beauty. Anger destroys wealth; tzedaka reveals the supernal colors in silver and gold and subdues the imagination (medameh). Pharaoh and Egypt are the aspect of imagination — the desire for money is Egypt's exile in every person and time. Holy money through tzedaka reveals G-d's greatness, subdues imagination, and elevates one above time. The prohibition of ribis (interest): taking payment for time strengthens imagination over intellect, equivalent to denying Hashem and the Exodus.

Entries 41–42: Commerce as cosmic clarification. The essential divine intent of all commerce is to clarify holy sparks and illuminate the supernal colors from one soul to another — therefore one must deal specifically with Israel. Through commerce one also merits nullifying time and ascending to the intellect (above time).

Entries 43–46: Loans, interest, and idolatry — Israel above time. The flow of money comes from the root of one's soul; borrowing creates a soul-subjugation. Idolatry is called a "debt" — therefore one must avoid being indebted, and ribis (interest) is equivalent to denying Hashem and worshipping idolatry. True gemilas chassadim sweetens the judgment of the borrower by illuminating life and holy faces upon them. Israel are by nature above time and thus distant from loans at their root — loans only exist because flow is delayed by time; above time all flow is always present. Taking interest for the time of waiting uproots flow from its root above time.

Entries 47–50: Time, anxiety, and the manna aspect. The essential livelihood anxiety is from time — worrying about tomorrow. Money flows from the north/left where foolishness holds. The remedy: realize there is no time, say "Blessed be Hashem day by day," and midnight rising is especially propitious for livelihood. Torah and holy livelihood need each other: money drawn through proper faith flows from the holy hairs of the beard (mazal), while money-desire draws from refuse-hairs of the Sitra Achra.

Entries 51–55: The tzaddik as universal conduit of wealth. All the world's wealth flows through the true tzaddik — the aspect of Yosef. The tzaddik draws wealth through sipurei ma'asiyos (stories): silver from stories clothing the Torah's faces, gold from ancient stories. Since the final Redemption comes through these stories, Israel will not be redeemed through silver but gold. The supreme mazal (Atika) is the root of all livelihood — it is all right with no left. The tzaddik must carefully dip into the left to form the flow as wealth while immediately including left in right. Without the true tzaddik-Moshe, the Reed Sea cannot be split for us — only through faith in Hashem and the tzaddik does one merit Torah and livelihood.

Entries 56–57: Servitude, time, freedom, and sanctifying possessions. All servitude is under time — the nations are essentially servants, Israel are essentially free because they received the Torah which is above time. One who pursues money permanence enslaves themselves. The serpent's defilement — the vision of this world — holds most strongly in money and attacks after every nullification experience. The remedy: sanctify all 39 melachos as Mishkan-work, bind the trace-light of every nullification into all one's possessions — then enormous flow can come without harm.

Entries 58–60: Commerce clarifies imagination; livelihood from afar; soul and body, grain and abundance. All commerce exists to clarify the imagination — the tzaddik's purchase is equivalent to fulfilling the Ten Commandments. Livelihood comes from the supreme mazal — extraordinarily far — all by Hashem's pure kindness. Both the wealthy (not to be arrogant) and the poor (not to worry) must internalize this. When Israel elevates soul over body, grain is blessed and nations are subdued; famine is Israel's disgrace as it indicates body overpowering soul.
